stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 2.3 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 294 K and 0.96 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 33.0 mL of 0.13 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.4 \times 10^{-4}) with 0.19 M NaOH.
5 g of $$\ce{NaOH}$$ dissolves in 123 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises by 9.7 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Mg electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and a Ni electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Ni^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e- -> Mg}$$ E° = -2.37 V; $$\ce{Ni^{2+} + 2e- -> Ni}$$ E° = -0.25 V.
The photoelectron spectra of C (Z = 6) and N (Z = 7) are compared.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.01 M solution of $$\ce{HNO3}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] equals its concentration.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 8.7 g. The actual yield is 7 g. What is the percent yield?
How many formula units or molecules are in 29 g of $$\ce{HNO3}$$?

options.why: Correct. Convert grams to moles, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

questions.stem: Why are metals good conductors of electricity?

options.text: Their ions move freely in the solid
options.why: Ions are fixed in the lattice.

options.text: Their valence electrons are delocalized and free to move

questions.stem: Under which conditions does a real gas deviate most from ideal behavior?

options.why: Correct. Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.explanation: Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.stem: Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 386 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: How can an unfavorable reaction (ΔG positive) be made to occur?

options.text: By coupling it to a favorable reaction so the total ΔG is negative

questions.stem: In HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺, which species is the Brønsted–Lowry base?
21 mL of 6.9 M solution is diluted to 304 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 4.3. A mixture has [A] = 0.9 M, [B] = 0.3 M and [C] = 0.3 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.333
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.333
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.333, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 1.11

questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH negative, which change shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃?

options.why: Correct. The product side has fewer moles of gas.
The reaction is exothermic; heating shifts left.

questions.explanation: The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.stem: Why is HI a stronger acid than HF?

options.text: F is less electronegative than I
The H–I bond is weaker and I⁻ is larger, so H⁺ is released more easily
options.why: Correct. Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.explanation: Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.stem: Which change alters the value of K?
What is the molecular geometry of $$\ce{CH4}$$?

options.why: Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.
Correct. Count electron domains and lone pairs on the central atom.
Lone pairs change the molecular shape from the electron-domain geometry.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of manganese (Mn, Z = 25)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 25 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 688 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 3 L flask at 5.59 atm and 435 K?
135 g of water at 79 °C is mixed with 140 g of water at 7 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.2).

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
He has a larger molar mass (4 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: N2 28, H2 2.02, He 4, CO2 44.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 7. What is K for the reaction multiplied by ½?

options.why: Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
O2 has a larger molar mass (32 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: N2 28, H2 2.02, O2 32, Ar 40.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{SO2}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$ is consumed at 0.87 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{H2O}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 6/5.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.5 mol N₂, 0.3 mol O₂ and 0.4 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4.9 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: 34 mL of 10.5 M solution is diluted to 396 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: A 28.7 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 26.8 mL of 0.19 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: In a mechanism, a species that is produced in one step and consumed in a later step is a(n):

options.why: Correct. It does not appear in the overall equation.
A catalyst is consumed first and regenerated later.

questions.explanation: It does not appear in the overall equation.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 101 kJ/mol, the transition state at 184 kJ/mol and the products at 7 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse Ea = transition state − products.
Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 83, ΔH = -94, reverse Ea = 177 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 10.7. In a solution at pH 12.7, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 1.36 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 242 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
A mass spectrum of a sample of chlorine shows two peaks: mass 35 with relative abundance 82% and mass 37 with 18%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Pair each mass with its own abundance.
Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0198 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0315 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
What is the oxidation number of C in $$\ce{CH4}$$?

options.why: Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{CaO}$$ or $$\ce{NaCl}$$?

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{CaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{NaCl}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{NaCl}$$, because its ions have larger charges

questions.explanation: CaO has ion charges 2 and 2; NaCl has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{CaF2}$$ is 3.9 \times 10^{-11}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 421 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: A 17.3 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 42 mL of 0.134 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 6.3. In a solution at pH 9.2, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A solid melts at 1,710 °C, is very hard and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely:

options.text: An ionic solid that conducts as a solid
options.why: Ionic solids do not conduct as solids.
Molecular solids melt at low temperatures.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of hydrofluoric acid (Ka = 6.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].
A weak acid does not ionize completely.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$$, 61 g of $$\ce{C3H8}$$ reacts with 73 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{CO2}$$ can form?

options.why: Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Zn/$$\ce{Zn^{2+}}$$ and Cu/$$\ce{Cu^{2+}}$$ half-cells. Which electrode is the anode?

options.why: The higher potential is reduced at the cathode.

options.text: Cu, where reduction occurs at the anode
options.why: Reduction occurs at the cathode, not the anode.
Correct. The half-reaction with the lower reduction potential runs as oxidation at the anode.

questions.explanation: Zn (E° -0.76 V) is oxidized at the anode; Cu is reduced at the cathode.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.38 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 6.35) and 0.26 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -141 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = 83 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -13 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 5.25; K = 190. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 4.87) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 9.86 mL. What is the pH after 4.93 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -5 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 2.02; K = 7.52. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.051 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 108 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 6.3 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 2840 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
Divide by the moles of reactant.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of Fe in $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$?

options.why: That is the percent of the other elements.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
There are 2 atoms of Fe in the formula.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 31 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 100 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 403 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).
Convert ΔS from J to kJ.

questions.stem: A compound (tetraphosphorus decoxide) is 43.6% P, 56.4% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to P2O5; the molecular formula is P4O10.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 524, 849, 4245, 7556 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 2 electrons, so it has 2 valence electrons.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$$.

options.why: Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.8 M and [I₂] = 1.2 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 1.84 M. What is K?
46 mL of 0.25 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.18 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches the equivalence point?

options.why: Correct. Moles of base = moles of acid.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 1; doubling [B] multiplies it by 4.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Recheck how the rate changes when [A] doubles.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×1, so order 0 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×4, so order 2 in B.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 0.468 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in ln[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: X → Y + Z. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Exothermic: the solution warmed, so energy was released.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Mg²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.05 M OH⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: Solubility increases: H⁺ reacts with OH⁻ (a base), shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of N.
Explain why the 1s peak of N has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of C.

rubric.criterion: N has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: N has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: C: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
